topic: Mastering the Product and Chain Rules in Calculus

outline.topic: Mastering the Product and Chain Rules in Calculus

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Rates
sections.content: Brief review of the derivative as an instantaneous rate of change. Introduce a visual analogy: a robot moving along a path. If the robot's speed is the derivative, how do we find the speed when two factors or nested functions are involved?
sections.example: Visualizing a speedometer on a robot changing based on its battery output (internal function) and the terrain slope (external function).

sections.title: The Product Rule: When Factors Multiply
sections.content: Explain that when two functions f(x) and g(x) are multiplied, the derivative is NOT just the product of derivatives. Use a 'geometric area' animation: as a rectangle grows in width and height simultaneously, the area change depends on both sides.
sections.example: Calculating the total weight gain of a growing puppy (f(t) = size, g(t) = density). The formula: (f*g)' = f'g + fg'.

sections.title: The Chain Rule: The 'Matryoshka' Principle
sections.content: Introduce the Chain Rule for composite functions f(g(x)). Use the 'nested boxes' or 'Russian Doll' visual metaphor. To find the rate of the outer shell, we must multiply it by the rate of the inner mechanism.
sections.example: A mechanical claw gripping an object: The claw opens (outer function) while the arm extends (inner function). Derivative = outer_derivative(inner) * inner_derivative.

sections.title: Synthesis & Complex Application
sections.content: Demonstrate a combined problem. Show how to identify which rule to apply first when a function has both products and nested layers. Visual hierarchy: Use color-coding to highlight the 'outer' vs 'inner' layers.
sections.example: Finding the derivative of f(x) = x^2 * sin(3x). Apply the Product Rule first, then use the Chain Rule to solve the derivative of sin(3x).

sections.title: Summary & Quick Check
sections.content: Review the mental checklist: 'Am I multiplying two terms?' (Product) vs 'Is one function inside another?' (Chain). Recap the two formulas side-by-side on screen.
sections.example: Final challenge: A 10-second flash quiz identifying the correct rule for three different equations.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Rates
lecture_lines: The derivative describes an instantaneous rate of change.
Visualize a robot moving along a path.
Speed depends on battery and terrain slope.
animations: Animate a car moving at a steady velocity #FF9900.
Show formula Rate = Change / Time in #00FFFF.

storyboard.title: The Product Rule: When Factors Multiply
lecture_lines: Product Rule applies to multiplying two functions.
Imagine a rectangle growing in both dimensions.
Area change depends on both width and height.
The rule: derivative is f'g plus fg'.
Total weight gain is the classic example.
animations: Show two functions f(x) and g(x) in #FFCC00.
Animate the expansion of the product f(x)g(x) in #00FF00.

storyboard.title: The Chain Rule: The 'Matryoshka' Principle
lecture_lines: Chain Rule handles composite, nested functions.
Think of it as the Matryoshka doll principle.
Derive the outer shell, then the inner mechanism.
Multiply rates to find the total change.
A mechanical claw demonstrates this perfectly.
animations: Animate nested boxes for f(g(x)) in #FF66FF.
Show derivative formula using composition in #00FFFF.

storyboard.title: Synthesis & Complex Application
lecture_lines: Complex functions combine product and chain rules.
Apply rules step-by-step with color coding.
animations: Combine Product and Chain rules on screen #FFFF00.
Highlight final unified derivative steps in #00FF00.

storyboard.title: Summary & Quick Check
lecture_lines: Multiply two terms? Use the Product Rule.
One function inside another? Use Chain Rule.
Check your understanding with our final quiz.
animations: Review key formulas one by one in #FF9900.
